# Data cleaning {#sec-m1-limpeza}

In analyses with administrative data, cleaning takes more time than the analysis. The difference
between doing it in a spreadsheet and doing it in R is that here the cleaning is **written down**: when the dataset
is updated next year, you just run it again. And anyone can audit what was
done.

The ANTAQ dataset we use is a good case because, in 732 rows, it has almost every problem
you will meet in real datasets.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readxl)

colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2",
             "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem",
             "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino",
             "tku")

bruto <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx")
stopifnot(ncol(bruto) == length(colunas))
names(bruto) <- colunas
```

## First diagnosis

Before fixing anything, look at the dataset. A five-command routine:

```{r}
dim(bruto)
sapply(bruto, class)
```

```{r}
colSums(is.na(bruto))            # declared missing values
```

```{r}
bruto |>
  dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), n_distinct)) |>
  t()
```

```{r}
summary(bruto$tku)
```

No `NA` and no negative value. But notice two odd things: the **minimum TKU is
zero** and there are only 2 distinct values in the `pais_origem` (country of origin) column, which should contain only
"Brasil" in a coastal shipping dataset.

```{r}
dplyr::count(bruto, pais_origem, pais_destino)
```

`janitor` has ready-made summaries that are very useful at this stage:

```{r}
#| eval: false
janitor::tabyl(bruto, uf_destino)     # frequency with percentage
skimr::skim(bruto)                    # full summary, column by column
```

## Disguised missing values

The `-` is the most common case of an **undeclared** missing value: it is not `NA`, it is text. Since the column
is text, R has no way of knowing that it means "no information".

```{r}
bruto |>
  dplyr::filter(pais_origem == "-") |>
  dplyr::count(tku_zero = tku == 0)
```

There are **120 rows** in which every identification field is `-` and the TKU is zero: they are
combinations of cargo profile and commodity group **with no flow** in the period, published
by the system as empty rows. They are neither a data error nor useful information for the analysis:
they are the table's "zero".

```{r}
bruto |> dplyr::filter(pais_origem == "-") |> dplyr::select(perfil, sh2, uf_origem, tku) |> head(3)
```

The right way to handle them: convert the `-` into `NA` explicitly, so that any later calculation
fails visibly instead of silently.

```{r}
base <- bruto |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), \(x) dplyr::na_if(stringr::str_squish(x), "-")))

colSums(is.na(base))
```

Now the missing values are declared. `readxl` and `readr` accept this instruction already when reading,
which is even better:

```{r}
#| eval: false
readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-", "n/d", "..."))
```

A related precaution: in spreadsheets, numbers sometimes come as text with a decimal comma.
In that case the whole column is read as text.

```{r}
valores <- c("1250,75", "n/d", "-", "890,10")

tku_corrigido <- valores |>
  dplyr::na_if("n/d") |>
  dplyr::na_if("-") |>
  stringr::str_replace(",", ".") |>
  as.numeric()

tku_corrigido
sum(is.na(tku_corrigido))
```

**Always** check how many `NA`s the conversion created. If many appeared, the number format
was not what you assumed. And `as.numeric()` turned them into missing values without warning.

## True zeros

Setting the `-` rows aside, 12 rows remain with zero TKU and complete identification:

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::filter(tku == 0, !is.na(uf_destino)) |>
  dplyr::select(perfil, uf_origem, cidade_origem, uf_destino, cidade_destino, tku)
```

Here navigation was recorded, but the rounded TKU came out as zero (very small distances and tonnages).
The decision is analytical, not technical: for TKU sums, including or excluding them changes
nothing; for **counting active links**, including or excluding them changes the result. What matters
is to record the choice:

```{r}
base <- base |> dplyr::filter(tku > 0)
nrow(base)
```

## *Encoding*

The problem shows up like this: `São Gonçalo` read as `SÃ£o GonÃ§alo` (a UTF-8 file read as
Latin-1) or `S?o Gon?alo` (the reverse). It is frequent in extracts from legacy systems.

```{r}
readr::guess_encoding("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.csv", n_max = 1000)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# reading with the correct encoding
readr::read_csv2("arquivo.csv", locale = readr::locale(encoding = "latin1"))
read.csv2("arquivo.csv", fileEncoding = "latin1")

# converting a vector that has already been read
x <- iconv(x, from = "latin1", to = "UTF-8")
```

A quick check that there is no encoding garbage in the municipality names:

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(cidade_destino, "Ã|Â|�")) |>
  dplyr::distinct(cidade_destino) |>
  nrow()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
On Windows, save scripts in UTF-8 (`File > Save with Encoding > UTF-8`) and check
`Sys.getlocale("LC_CTYPE")`. In recent versions of R (4.2+) UTF-8 support on Windows has
improved a lot, but old files still come in Latin-1.
:::

## Standardising text

Before counting categories, standardise. Otherwise `"Paranaguá"`, `"PARANAGUÁ"` and `" Paranagua "`
count as three different ports.

```{r}
base <- base |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), str_squish),
    uf_origem  = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_origem),
    uf_destino = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_destino),
    chave_destino = cidade_destino |>
      stringr::str_to_lower() |>
      stringi::stri_trans_general("Latin-ASCII") |>
      stringr::str_squish()
  )

base |> dplyr::distinct(cidade_destino, chave_destino) |> head(4)
```

The `chave_destino` (destination key) column is not meant for reading. It is meant for **joining** with other datasets, in the
next chapter.

## Duplicates

There are two kinds: a whole row repeated (an extraction error) and a repeated **key** where it
should be unique (a conceptual error). The second is the dangerous one.

```{r}
sum(duplicated(base))        # identical rows
```

None. But which key should be unique? Test the most natural hypothesis: one pair of
facilities for each commodity.

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::count(instalacao_origem, instalacao_destino, sh2) |>
  dplyr::filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()
```

There are repetitions. Before "removing duplicates", investigate **one concrete case**:

```{r}
caso <- base |>
  dplyr::count(instalacao_origem, instalacao_destino, sh2) |>
  dplyr::filter(n > 1) |>
  dplyr::slice(1)

base |>
  dplyr::semi_join(caso, by = c("instalacao_origem", "instalacao_destino", "sh2")) |>
  dplyr::select(perfil, instalacao_origem, instalacao_destino, sh2, tku)
```

What sets the rows apart is the **cargo profile**: the same commodity, between the same
facilities, moved partly as general cargo and partly as bulk. In other words, the
real granularity of the dataset is *profile × commodity × origin facility × destination
facility*:

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::count(perfil, sh2, instalacao_origem, instalacao_destino) |>
  dplyr::filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()
```

Zero: the key is identified. This matters because it is what allows TKU to be summed in any
broader aggregation without counting anything twice.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# how to remove duplicates when they really are an error
base |> dplyr::distinct()                                          # identical rows
base |> dplyr::distinct(uf_origem, uf_destino, .keep_all = TRUE)   # 1st row of each key
base |> dplyr::slice_max(tku, n = 1, by = c(uf_origem, uf_destino), with_ties = FALSE)
base |> dplyr::summarise(tku = sum(tku), .by = c(uf_origem, uf_destino))  # aggregate
```

::: {.callout-important}
Never remove duplicates by reflex. First ask: **what is the unit of observation of this
table?** If the answer is "one row per profile, commodity and pair of facilities", then
aggregating is correct and removing is a loss of information.
:::

## *Outliers*

```{r}
q <- quantile(base$tku, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95, 0.99))
round(q / 1e6, 1)      # in millions of t·km

limite_sup <- q[["75%"]] + 3 * IQR(base$tku)

base |>
  dplyr::filter(tku > limite_sup) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(cidade_origem, uf_origem, cidade_destino, tku_bi = round(tku / 1e9, 1)) |>
  head(5)
```

In transport flows the distribution is strongly skewed: a few pairs concentrate most
of the TKU.

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(part = tku / sum(tku), part_acum = cumsum(part)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(cidade_origem, cidade_destino,
            part = scales::percent(part, accuracy = 0.1),
            part_acum = scales::percent(part_acum, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  head(10)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
An *outlier* in flow data is rarely an error. It is concentration. The largest links being an
order of magnitude above the median is a feature of the system, not a defect of the data. Treat
as an error only what is **impossible** (see below); for the rest, use a logarithmic scale in the
chart instead of excluding the observation.
:::

## Unrealistic and incorrect values, and special categories

This is the step that requires domain knowledge. Translate business rules into explicit
checks (negative TKU, year out of range, invalid state codes, country other than Brazil):

```{r}
ufs_validas <- c("AC","AL","AP","AM","BA","CE","DF","ES","GO","MA","MT","MS","MG","PA",
                 "PB","PR","PE","PI","RJ","RN","RS","RO","RR","SC","SP","SE","TO")

base |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    tku_negativo    = sum(tku < 0),
    ano_fora        = sum(!ano %in% 2000:2026),
    uf_origem_fora  = sum(!uf_origem %in% ufs_validas),
    uf_destino_fora = sum(!uf_destino %in% ufs_validas),
    pais_nao_brasil = sum(pais_origem != "Brasil" | pais_destino != "Brasil")
  ) |>
  t()
```

The state check flagged rows. Before concluding there is an error, look at **which** values they are:

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::filter(!uf_origem %in% ufs_validas) |>
  dplyr::count(uf_origem, wt = tku / 1e9, name = "tku_bi") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi))
```

Two categories that are neither an error nor a state:

- **ZEE/Plat. Continental**: origin at sea, on the platforms of the Exclusive Economic Zone.
  These are **37 links** accounting for about **109 billion t·km**, almost 40% of the total
  TKU: it is the oil leaving the platforms for the terminals on the mainland. Excluding these
  rows as an "invalid state" would destroy the largest component of the dataset.
- **Indeterminado** (undetermined): origin not identified in the record.

The right treatment is to create a column that makes these categories **explicit**, instead of
deleting them (offshore, undetermined, intrastate, interstate):

```{r}
cabotagem <- base |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    origem_offshore = uf_origem == "ZEE/PLAT. CONTINENTAL",
    origem_indefinida = uf_origem == "INDETERMINADO",
    tipo_ligacao = dplyr::case_when(
      origem_offshore   ~ "offshore",
      origem_indefinida ~ "indeterminada",
      uf_origem == uf_destino ~ "intraestadual",
      .default = "interestadual"
    ),
    tku_bi = tku / 1e9
  )

cabotagem |>
  dplyr::summarise(ligacoes = dplyr::n(), tku_bi = round(sum(tku_bi), 1), .by = tipo_ligacao) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi))
```

This table is, on its own, a result worth a paragraph in a report: 38% of Brazilian
coastal shipping TKU **does not leave from a port on land**, but from offshore platforms.

::: {.callout-note}
## The lesson of the chapter

Cleaning is not "deleting what does not fit". Both times the data looked wrong
(the repeated keys and the invalid states), the investigation revealed **structure**: an
extra dimension (cargo profile) and a legitimate category (offshore). What gets deleted without
investigation is precisely what tends to be most informative.
:::

## The complete cleaning script

Putting it all together, what we hand over to the next chapters:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 02-limpeza.R: ANTAQ coastal shipping (TB6.1)
# Input:  dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx
# Output: dados/cabotagem_limpa.rds
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(dplyr); library(stringr); library(readxl)

colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2",
             "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem",
             "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino",
             "tku")

cabotagem <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-"))
stopifnot(ncol(cabotagem) == length(colunas))
names(cabotagem) <- colunas

cabotagem <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), str_squish)) |>
  dplyr::filter(tku > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    uf_origem  = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_origem),
    uf_destino = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_destino),
    tku_bi = tku / 1e9,
    tipo_ligacao = dplyr::case_when(
      uf_origem == "ZEE/PLAT. CONTINENTAL" ~ "offshore",
      uf_origem == "INDETERMINADO"         ~ "indeterminada",
      uf_origem == uf_destino              ~ "intraestadual",
      .default = "interestadual"
    )
  )

# safeguards: if the dataset changes, the script stops here
stopifnot(
  nrow(cabotagem) == 600,
  all(cabotagem$tku > 0),
  all(cabotagem$pais_destino == "Brasil"),
  dplyr::n_distinct(cabotagem[c("perfil", "sh2", "instalacao_origem",
                         "instalacao_destino")]) == nrow(cabotagem)
)

saveRDS(cabotagem, "dados/cabotagem_limpa.rds")
```

The `stopifnot()` with the expected number of rows deserves a comment: it **will fail**
next year, when the dataset is updated. And that is the goal. The failure forces you to review the
number and confirm the change was expected, instead of publishing a report with a different
total without anyone noticing.
